question: in which conditions does selective availability (a shared stage) beat an ordinary rival that learns whom to ask, at the same bandwidth?
grid: slots {20,40,80} x cross {0.10,0.25,0.50} x noise {0.3,0.6,0.9}, 27 cells, seed 30000 + cell index, 100 independent histories per cell

primary.measure: total = mean(transfer accuracy, own accuracy), paired by history, bootstrap 95% CI
primary.rule: a stage arm PAYS in a cell when its mean contrast >= +0.05 and the CI lower bound > 0; it COSTS when the mean <= -0.05 and the CI upper bound < 0; otherwise NEUTRAL. reported per cell and per arm. the grid's best_stage_minus_local (per-history max of two arms) is biased toward the stage and is NOT used for any verdict.

secondary: temporal - single_winner on total and on revision accuracy (does keeping the alternative help revision?)
random_stage vs single_winner (does selection matter, or only availability?)
oracle - none (the ceiling of the cell: a cell whose ceiling is under 0.05 cannot show a 0.05 effect and is marked UNINFORMATIVE)
prediction: stage arms PAY only where memory is ample (slots 80), crossing is high (0.50) and salience is accurate (noise 0.3); COST where memory is scarce (slots 20); temporal beats single_winner on revision but not on total
seen_before: smoke-1 (revision 1 world, seed 1) and smoke-2 (revision 2, seed 2, 30 histories) and grid-check (seed 1, 5 histories); they shaped the world and the grid, not these rules; their seeds are not reused
not_claimed: a toy world about when broadcast pays; nothing about experience, luna or any live system
